summary: Explains how Service Location Protocol version 2 can be extended by vendors safely, without name collisions, by adding a Vendor Opaque Extension. It aims to let proprietary additions coexist without breaking interoperability. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Companies sometimes want to add their own special features. This gives them a labeled spot to put those extras so they do not confuse other products.

questions: what is the slp vendor opaque extension
what is an enterprise number in slp
what is an slp naming authority
subtitle: How vendors can add their own features to Service Location Protocol version 2 without clashing with anyone else.

tldr.problem: Vendors sometimes want to extend SLPv2 privately, but two vendors could pick the same service type, attribute name or extension ID and create ambiguity.
tldr.mechanism: Vendors use their IANA Enterprise Number as a naming authority, in attribute names (x- plus the number), and in a new Vendor Opaque Extension (ID 0x0003) that carries a 4-byte Enterprise Number before the vendor's own data.
tldr.outcome: Vendor additions can coexist without collisions, though the RFC stresses that registering service templates with IANA is the better path. Any other change to SLPv2 needs a standards action.

today: RFC 3224 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2608. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Vendor Extensions Need Rules
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol, Version 2 (SLPv2, RFC 2608) has several features that can be extended. This document clarifies exactly which mechanisms may be used for that and which may not, and it updates RFC 2608 with conventions that stop extension mechanisms from having ambiguous meanings.

It adds only one new protocol element, the Vendor Opaque Extension. A vendor that has registered with IANA and obtained an Enterprise Number can use it to extend SLP on its own, which is useful for vendor-specific applications.

The RFC is frank about the cost. Vendor extensions are not reviewed by the community, they prevent interoperation with compliant but non-extended implementations, and private extensions make ubiquitous automatic configuration impossible. For these reasons it strongly encourages registering service templates with IANA, a process it says usually takes less than 2 weeks.
sections.eli5: Companies sometimes want to add their own special tricks. That is allowed, but it can make their gadgets stop understanding other gadgets, so there are rules to keep things tidy.

sections.title: Enterprise Numbers and Naming Authorities
sections.content:
Enterprise Numbers distinguish vendors in IETF protocols. Vendor extensions to SLPv2 SHOULD use them to avoid any name space collision, and each vendor is responsible for keeping its own extensions non-conflicting. IANA keeps the list of 'SMI Network Management Private Enterprise Codes' under 1.3.6.1.4.1, and a number can be registered through an on-line form.

A Naming Authority is an agency or group that catalogues service types and attributes. Service types and attributes can be registered with IANA by writing a Service Template, in which case IANA is the naming authority. A vendor can instead act as its own naming authority by using its Enterprise Number as the authority string. Service types and attributes defined that way are guaranteed not to conflict with others.

The RFC's fictitious example uses Enterprise Number 9999 for Acme, Inc., giving a URL such as service:roadrunner-detector.9999://example.com:9341.
sections.eli5: Each company gets a unique number, like a locker number. If you put your number on your labels, nobody can mistake your label for someone else's.

sections.title: Vendor Defined Attributes
sections.content:
SLPv2 suggests that non-standard attribute names SHOULD begin with x-, since no standard attribute name will ever start that way. Two vendors could still both pick the same x- name, so this RFC says vendors SHOULD write the x- prefix, then their Enterprise Number, then a hyphen, so the meaning is never ambiguous.

In the RFC's example, a Service Template for a fictitious game called NetHive lists standard features. Acme's server also advertises x-9999-cheat-mode. Only an Acme client would ask for that attribute, because it is not standard.
sections.eli5: If you invent a secret nickname, put your locker number in front of it. Then your nickname cannot be confused with a friend's.

sections.title: The Vendor Opaque Extension
sections.content:
SLPv2 extensions are added at the end of a message. Each starts with a 16-bit Extension ID and a Next Extension Offset, followed by Extension Data whose format depends on the ID. The RFC lists three ways to extend SLPv2.

  • Ask the designated expert for SLP to register a new extension ID with IANA. An Internet Draft is recommended, ideally leading to an Informational RFC. This is the preferred vendor-neutral way.
  • Use an experimental ID in the range 0x8000 to 0x8FFF. These IDs are not registered, so another vendor might pick the same one.
  • Use the Vendor Extension, which gives a vendor extensions with a guaranteed unique interpretation. Implementing it is OPTIONAL.

The Vendor Opaque Extension uses Extension ID 0x0003. After the offset comes the Enterprise Number as a 4-byte unsigned integer, then the Extension Data, which the vendor alone defines.
sections.eli5: There is a special envelope with the company's locker number on the front. Whatever is inside is for that company only, and everyone else just ignores it.

sections.title: Example: Acme Authentication Extension
sections.content:
The RFC sketches how Acme (Enterprise Number 9999) might use the extension for application-level access control, so replies go only to clients who can authenticate. Acme's extension data starts with a one-byte ACME Ext ID, set to 1 for this extension, which would let Acme define up to 256 different extensions. Next come a Client ID Length, the Client ID, a Timestamp (seconds since January 1, 2000, 0:00 GMT) and an Authenticator.

The Authenticator is a 16-byte MD5 digest over the request bytes (header but no extensions), a secret pass phrase, the Client ID and the Timestamp. An SA or DA receiving it checks that it recognizes the Client ID, has a pass phrase for it, and computes the same digest.

The RFC says this is for explanation only and would not work well in practice: it needs a shared secret configured for every UA, and the pass phrase would be open to a dictionary attack.
sections.eli5: Acme invents a secret handshake: show your name, the time and a scrambled stamp made with a shared password. The RFC admits it is only a made-up example.

sections.title: Limits, IANA and Security
sections.content:
Modifying or extending any other feature of SLPv2 aside from the mechanisms above requires a standards action. The Vendor Opaque Extension ID has already been registered, so no IANA action is needed for this document.

On security, the RFC notes that vendor extensions may introduce new security considerations. The only mechanism it describes is no less secure than the 'private use' extensions already defined in SLPv2. The Acme example shows how a vendor could add an access control mechanism, but protocol details were intentionally left out.
sections.eli5: Anything beyond these tidy rules needs the grown-ups to agree first. Adding your own extras can bring new risks, so be careful.

fields.name: Extension ID
fields.desc: Set to 0x0003 for the Vendor Opaque Extension.

fields.name: Next Extension Offset
fields.desc: Offset to the next extension, if any.

fields.name: Enterprise Number
fields.desc: The vendor's IANA Enterprise Number, a 4-byte unsigned integer.

fields.name: Extension Data
fields.desc: Vendor-defined data with an unambiguous meaning set by the vendor (variable length).
